breaths.text: An amusement park on the outskirts of Budapest on a late afternoon in Spring.
Barkers stand before the booths of the sideshows haranguing the passing crowd.
The strident music of a calliope is heard; laughter, shouts, the scuffle of feet, the signal bells of merry-go-round.
The merry-go-round is at Center.
LILIOM stands at the entrance, a cigarette in his mouth, coaxing the people in.
The girls regard him with idolizing glances and screech with pleasure as he playfully pushes them through entrance.

Now and then some girl's escort resents the familiarity, whereupon LILIOM'S demeanor becomes ugly and menacing, and the cowed escort slinks through the entrance behind his girl or contents himself with a muttered resentful comment.
One girl hands LILIOM a red carnation; he rewards her with a bow and a smile.
When the soldier who accompanies her protests, LILIOM cows him with a fierce glance and a threatening gesture.
MARIE and JULIE come out of the crowd and LILIOM favors them with particular notice as they pass into the merry-go-round.
MRS. MUSKAT comes out of the merry-go-round, bringing LILIOM coffee and rolls.
LILIOM mounts the barker's stand at the entrance, where he is elevated over everyone on the stage.
Here he begins his harangue.
Everybody turns toward him.
The other booths are gradually deserted.
The tumult makes it impossible for the audience to hear what he is saying, but every now and then some witticism of his provokes a storm of laughter which is audible above the din.
Many people enter the merry-go-round.
Here and there one catches a phrase "Room for one more on the zebra's back," "Which of you ladies?"
"Ten heller for adults, five for children," "Step right up"---It is growing darker.
A lamplighter crosses the stage, and begins unperturbedly lighting the colored gas-lamps.
The whistle of a distant locomotive is heard.
Suddenly the tumult ceases, the lights go out, and the curtain falls in darkness.
SCENE--_A lonely place in the park, half hidden by trees and shrubbery.
Under a flowering acacia tree stands a painted wooden bench.
From the distance, faintly, comes the tumult of the amusement park.
It is the sunset of the same day._
_When the curtain rises the stage is empty._
_MARIE enters quickly, pauses at center, and looks back._
Marie: Julie, Julie!
Marie: [_There is no answer._] Do you hear me, Julie?
Marie: Let her be!
Marie: Come on.
Marie: Let her be.
Marie: [_Starts to go back._] [_JULIE enters, looks back angrily._] JULIE Did you ever hear of such a thing?
Marie: What's the matter with the woman anyway?
[_Looking back again._]
Marie: Here she comes again.
Julie: Let her come.
Julie: I didn't do anything to her.
Julie: All of a sudden she comes up to me and begins to raise a row.
Marie: Here she is.
Marie: Come on, let's run.
Marie: [_Tries to urge her off._] JULIE Run?
Marie: I should say not.
Marie: What would I want to run for?
Marie: I'm not afraid of her.
Marie: Oh, come on.
Marie: She'll only start a fight.
Julie: I'm going to stay right here.
Julie: Let her _start_ a fight.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT [_Entering._] What do you want to run away for?
Julie: [_To JULIE._] Don't worry.
Julie: I won't eat you.
Julie: But there's one thing I want to tell you, my dear.
Julie: Don't let me catch you in my carousel again.
Julie: I stand for a whole lot, I have to in my business.
Julie: It makes no difference to me whether my customers are ladies or the likes of you--as long as they pay their money.
Julie: But when a girl misbehaves herself on my carousel--out she goes.
Julie: Do you understand?
Julie: Are you talking to me?
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Yes, you!
Julie: You--chamber-maid, you!
Julie: In my carousel----
Julie: Who did anything in your old carousel?
Julie: I paid my fare and took my seat and never said a word, except to my friend here.
Marie: No, she never opened her mouth.
Marie: Liliom came over to her of his own accord.
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT It's all the same.
Marie: I'm not going to get in trouble with the police, and lose my license on account of you--you shabby kitchen maid!
Julie: Shabby yourself.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT You stay out of my carousel!
Julie: Letting my barker fool with you!
Julie: Aren't you ashamed of yourself?
Julie: What?
Julie: What did you say?
Julie: I suppose you think I have no eyes in my head.
Julie: I see everything that goes on in my carousel.
Julie: During the whole ride she let Liliom fool with her--the shameless hussy!
Julie: He did not fool with me!
Julie: I don't let any man fool with me!
Julie: He leaned against you all through the ride!
Julie: He leaned against the panther.
Julie: He always leans against something, doesn't he?
Julie: Everybody leans where he wants.
Julie: I couldn't tell him not to lean, if he always leans, could I?
Julie: But he didn't lay a hand on me.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Oh, didn't he?
Julie: And I suppose he didn't put his hand around your waist, either?
Marie: And if he did?
Marie: What of it?
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT You hold your tongue!
Marie: No one's asking you--just you keep out of it.
Julie: He put his arm around my waist--just the same as he does to all the girls.
Julie: He always does that.
Julie: I'll teach him not to do it any more, my dear.
Julie: No carryings on in my carousel!
Julie: If you are looking for that sort of thing, you'd better go to the circus!
Julie: You'll find lots of soldiers there to carry on with!
Julie: You keep your soldiers for yourself!
Marie: Soldiers!
Marie: As if we wanted soldiers!
Marie: Well, I only want to tell you this, my dear, so that we understand each other perfectly.
Marie: If you ever stick your nose in my carousel again, you'll wish you hadn't!
Marie: I'm not going to lose my license on account of the likes of you!
Marie: People who don't know how to behave, have got to stay out!
Julie: You're wasting your breath.
Julie: If I feel like riding on your carousel I'll pay my ten heller and I'll ride.
Julie: I'd like to see anyone try to stop me!
Julie: Just come and try it, my dear--just come and try it.
Marie: We'll see what'll happen.
Marie: Yes, you will see something happen that never happened before in this park.
Julie: Perhaps you think you could throw me out!
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT I'm sure of it, my dear.
Julie: And suppose I'm stronger than you?
Julie: I'd think twice before I'd dirty my hands on a common servant girl.
Julie: I'll have Liliom throw you out.
Julie: He knows how to handle your kind.
Julie: You think Liliom would throw me out.
Julie: Yes, my dear, so fast that you won't know what happened to you!
Julie: He'd throw me---- [_Stops suddenly, for MRS. MUSKAT has turned away.
Julie: Both look off stage until LILIOM enters, surrounded by four giggling servant girls._] LILIOM Go away!
Julie: Stop following me, or I'll smack your face!
Julie: Well, give me back my handkerchief.
Liliom: Go on now----
Liliom: THE FOUR SERVANT GIRLS [_Simultaneously._] What do you think of him?--My handkerchief!--Give it back to her!--That's a nice thing to do!
Liliom: THE LITTLE SERVANT GIRL [_To MRS. MUSKAT._] Please, lady, make him---MRS. MUSKAT Oh, shut up!
Liliom: Will you get out of here?
Liliom: [_Makes a threatening gesture--the four servant girls exit in voluble but fearful haste._] MRS. MUSKAT What have you been doing now?
Liliom: None of your business.
Liliom: [_Glances at JULIE._] Have you been starting with her again?
Julie: Mister Liliom, please----
[_Steps threateningly toward her._]
Liliom: Don't yell!
[_Timidly._]
Julie: I didn't yell.
Liliom: Well, don't.
Liliom: [_To MRS. MUSKAT._] What's the matter?
Liliom: What has she done to you?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT What has she done?
Liliom: She's been impudent to me.
Liliom: Just as impudent as she could be!
Liliom: I put her out of the carousel.
Liliom: Take a good look at this innocent thing, Liliom.
Liliom: She's never to be allowed in my carousel again!
[_To JULIE._]
Liliom: You heard that.
Liliom: Run home, now.
Marie: Come on.
Marie: Don't waste your time with such people.
Marie: [_Tries to lead JULIE away._] JULIE No, I won't---MRS. MUSKAT If she ever comes again, you're not to let her in.
Marie: And if she gets in before you see her, throw her out.
Marie: Understand?
Liliom: What has she done, anyhow?
[_Agitated and very earnest._]
Julie: Mister Liliom--tell me please--honest and truly--if I come into the carousel, will you throw me out?
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Of course he'll throw you out.
Marie: She wasn't talking to you.
Julie: Tell me straight to my face, Mister Liliom, would you throw me out?
[_They face each other.
There is a brief pause._]
Liliom: Yes, little girl, if there was a reason--but if there was no reason, why should I throw you out?
[_To MRS. MUSKAT._]
Marie: There, you see!
Julie: Thank you, Mister Liliom.
Julie: And I tell you again, if this little slut dares to set her foot in my carousel, she's to be thrown out!
Julie: I'll stand for no indecency in my establishment.
Liliom: What do you mean--indecency?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT I saw it all.
Liliom: There's no use denying it.
Julie: She says you put your arm around my waist.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Yes, you!
Julie: I saw you.
Julie: Don't play the innocent.
Liliom: Here's something new!
Liliom: I'm not to put my arm around a girl's waist any more!
Liliom: I suppose I'm to ask your permission before I touch another girl!
Liliom: You can touch as many girls as you want and as often as you want--for my part you can go as far as you like with any of them--but not this one--I permit no indecency in my carousel.
Liliom: [_There is a long pause._] LILIOM [_To MRS. MUSKAT._] And now I'll ask you please to shut your mouth.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT What?
Liliom: Shut your mouth quick, and go back to your carousel.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT What?
Liliom: What did she do to you, anyhow?
Liliom: Tryin' to start a fight with a little pigeon like that . . . just because I touched her?--You come to the carousel as often as you want to, little girl.
Liliom: Come every afternoon, and sit on the panther's back, and if you haven't got the price, Liliom will pay for you.
Liliom: And if anyone dares to bother you, you come and tell _me._ MRS. MUSKAT You reprobate!
Liliom: Old witch!
Julie: Thank you, Mister Liliom.
Julie: You seem to think that I can't throw you out, too.
Julie: What's the reason I can't?
Julie: Because you are the best barker in the park?
Julie: Well, you are very much mistaken.
Julie: In fact, you can consider yourself thrown out already.
Julie: You're discharged!
Liliom: Very good.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Weakening a little._] I can discharge you any time I feel like it.
Liliom: Very good, you feel like discharging me.
Liliom: I'm discharged.
Liliom: That settles it.
Liliom: Playing the high and mighty, are you?
Liliom: Conceited pig!
Liliom: Good-for-nothing!
Liliom: You said you'd throw me out, didn't you?
Liliom: Well, that suits me; I'm thrown out.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Softening._] Do you have to take up every word I say?
Liliom: It's all right; it's all settled.
Liliom: I'm a good-for-nothing.
Liliom: And a conceited pig.
Liliom: And I'm discharged.
Liliom: Do you want to ruin my business?
Liliom: A good-for-nothing?
Liliom: Now I know!
Liliom: And I'm discharged!
Liliom: Very good.
Liliom: You're a devil, you are . . . and that woman---LILIOM Keep away from her!
Liliom: I'll get Hollinger to give you such a beating that you'll hear all the angels sing . . . and it won't be the first time, either.
Liliom: Get out of here.
Liliom: I'm discharged.
Liliom: And you get out of here.
[_Timidly._]
Julie: Mister Liliom, if she's willing to say that she hasn't discharged you---LILIOM You keep out of this.
[_Timidly._]
Julie: I don't want this to happen on account of me.
[_To MRS. MUSKAT, pointing to JULIE._]
Liliom: Apologize to her!
Marie: A-ha!
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT Apologize?
Marie: To who? LILIOM To this little pigeon.
Marie: Well--are you going to do it?

Marie: If you give me this whole park on a silver plate, and all the gold of the Rothschilds on top of it--I'd--I'd---- Let her dare to come into my carousel again and she'll get thrown out so hard that she'll see stars in daylight!

Liliom: In that case, dear lady [_takes off his cap with a flourish_], you are respectfully requested to get out o' here as fast as your legs will carry you--I never beat up a woman yet--except that Holzer woman who I sent to the hospital for three weeks--but--if you don't get out o' here this minute, and let this little squab be, I'll give you the prettiest slap in the jaw you ever had in your life.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Very good, my son.
Liliom: Now you _can_ go to the devil.
Liliom: Good-bye.
Liliom: You're discharged, and you needn't try to come back, either.
[_She exits.
It is beginning to grow dark._]
[_With grave concern._]
Marie: Mister Liliom----
Liliom: Don't you pity me or I'll give _you_ a slap in the jaw.
Liliom: [_To JULIE._] And don't you pity me, either.
[_In alarm._]
Julie: I don't pity you, Mister Liliom.
Liliom: You're a liar, you _are_ pitying me.
Liliom: I can see it in your face.
Liliom: You're thinking, now that Madame Muskat has thrown him out, Liliom will have to go begging.
Liliom: Huh! Look at me.
Liliom: I'm big enough to get along without a Madame Muskat.
Liliom: I have been thrown out of better jobs than hers.
Julie: What will you do now, Mister Liliom?
Liliom: Now?
Liliom: First of all, I'll go and get myself--a glass of beer.
Liliom: You see, when something happens to annoy me, I always drink a glass of beer.
Julie: Then you _are_ annoyed about losing your job.
Liliom: No, only about where I'm going to get the beer.
Marie: Well--eh----
Liliom: Well--eh--what?
Marie: Well--eh--are you going to stay with us, Mister Liliom?
Liliom: Will you pay for the beer?
Liliom: [_MARIE looks doubtful; he turns to JULIE._] Will you?
Liliom: [_She does not answer._] How much money have you got?
[_Bashfully._]
Julie: Eight heller.
Liliom: And you?
[_MARIE casts down her eyes and does not reply.
Liliom: LILIOM continues sternly._] I asked you how much you've got?
Liliom: [_MARIE begins to weep softly._] I understand.
Liliom: Well, you needn't cry about it.
Liliom: You girls stay here, while I go back to the carousel and get my clothes and things.
Liliom: And when I come back, we'll go to the Hungarian beer-garden.
Liliom: It's all right, I'll pay.
Liliom: Keep your money.
[_He exits.
Liliom: MARIE and JULIE stand silent, watching him until he has gone._] MARIE Are you sorry for him?
Julie: Are you?
Marie: Yes, a little.
Marie: Why are you looking after him in that funny way?
[_Sits down._]
Julie: Nothing--except I'm sorry he lost his job.
[_With a touch of pride._]
Marie: It was on our account he lost his job.
Marie: Because he's fallen in love with you.
Julie: He hasn't at all.
[_Confidently._]
Marie: Oh, yes! he is in love with you.
Marie: [_Hesitantly, romantically._] There is someone in love with me, too.
Julie: There is?
Julie: Who? MARIE
Julie: I--I never mentioned it before, because you hadn't a lover of your own--but now you have--and I'm free to speak.
Julie: [_Very grandiloquently._] My heart has found its mate.
Julie: You're only making it up.
Marie: No, it's true--my heart's true love----
Julie: Who?
Julie: Who is he?
Marie: A soldier.
Julie: What kind of a soldier?
Marie: I don't know.
Marie: Just a soldier.
Marie: Are there different kinds?
Julie: Many different kinds.
Julie: There are hussars, artillerymen, engineers, infantry--that's the kind that walks--and---MARIE How can you tell which is which?
Julie: By their uniforms.
[_After trying to puzzle it out._]
Marie: The conductors on the street cars--are they soldiers?
Julie: Certainly not.
Julie: They're conductors.
Marie: Well, they have uniforms.
Julie: But they don't carry swords or guns.
Marie: Oh!
Marie: [_Thinks it over again; then._] Well, policemen--are they?
[_With a touch of exasperation._]
Julie: Are they what?
Marie: Soldiers.
Julie: Certainly not.
Julie: They're just policemen.
[_Triumphantly._]
Marie: But they have uniforms--and they carry weapons, too.
Julie: You're just as dumb as you can be.
Julie: You don't go by their uniforms.
Marie: But you said----
Julie: No, I didn't.
Julie: A letter-carrier wears a uniform, too, but that doesn't make him a soldier.
Marie: But if he carried a gun or a sword, would he be---JULIE No, he'd still be a letter-carrier.
Marie: You can't go by guns or swords, either.
Marie: Well, if you don't go by the uniforms or the weapons, what _do_ you go by?
Julie: By---- [_Tries to put it into words; fails; then breaks off suddenly._] Oh, you'll get to know when you've lived in the city long enough.
Julie: You're nothing but a country girl.
Julie: When you've lived in the city a year, like I have, you'll know all about it.
[_Half angrily._]
Marie: Well, how _do_ you know when _you_ see a real soldier?
Julie: By one thing.
Marie: What?
Julie: One thing---- [_She pauses.
Julie: MARIE starts to cry._] Oh, what are you crying about?
Marie: Because you're making fun of me. . . .
Marie: You're a city girl, and I'm just fresh from the country . . . and how am I expected to know a soldier when I see one? . . .
Marie: You, you ought to tell me, instead of making fun of me---JULIE All right.
Marie: Listen then, cry-baby.
Marie: There's only one way to tell a soldier: by his salute!
Marie: That's the only way.
[_Joyfully; with a sigh of relief._]
Marie: Ah--that's good.
Julie: What?
Marie: I say--it's all right then--because Wolf--Wolf---- [_JULIE laughs derisively._] Wolf--that's his name.
Marie: [_She weeps again._] JULIE Crying again?
Marie: What now?
Marie: You're making fun of me again.
Julie: I'm not.
Julie: But when you say, "Wolf--Wolf--" like that, I have to laugh, don't I?
Julie: [_Archly._] What's his name again?
Marie: I won't tell you.
Julie: All right.
Julie: If you won't say it, then he's no soldier.
Marie: I'll say it.
Julie: Go on.
Marie: No, I won't.
Marie: [_She weeps again._] JULIE Then he's not a soldier.
Marie: I guess he's a letter-carrier----
Marie: No--no--I'd rather say it.
Julie: Well, then.
[_Giggling._]
Marie: But you mustn't look at me.
Marie: You look the other way, and I'll say it.
Marie: [_JULIE looks away, MARIE can hardly restrain her own laughter._] Wolf!
Marie: [_She laughs._] That's his real name.
Marie: Wolf, Wolf, Soldier--Wolf!
Julie: What kind of a uniform does he wear?
Marie: Red.
Julie: Red trousers?
Marie: No.
Julie: Red coat?
Marie: No.
Julie: What then?
[_Triumphantly._]
Marie: His cap!
[_After a long pause._]
Julie: He's just a porter, you dunce.
Julie: Red cap . . . that's a porter--and he doesn't carry a gun or a sword, either.
[_Triumphantly._]
Marie: But he salutes.
Marie: You said yourself that was the only way to tell a soldier---JULIE He doesn't salute at all.
Marie: He only greets people----
Marie: He salutes me. . . .
Marie: And if his name _is_ Wolf, that doesn't prove he ain't a soldier--he salutes, and he wears a red cap and he stands on guard all day long outside a big building---JULIE What does he do there?
[_Seriously._]
Marie: He spits.
[_With contempt._]
Julie: He's nothing--nothing but a common porter.
Marie: What's Liliom?
[_Indignantly._]
Julie: Why speak of him?
Julie: What has he to do with me?
Marie: The same as Wolf has to do with me.
Marie: If you can talk to me like that about Wolf, I can talk to you about Liliom.
Julie: He's nothing to me.
Julie: He put his arm around me in the carousel.
Julie: I couldn't tell him not to put his arm around me after he had done it, could I?
Marie: I suppose you didn't like him to do it?
Julie: No.
Marie: Then why are you waiting for him?
Marie: Why don't you go home?
Julie: Why--eh--he _said_ we were to wait for him.
[_LILIOM enters.
There is a long silence._]
Liliom: Are you still here?
Liliom: What are you waiting for?
Marie: You told us to wait.
Liliom: Must you always interfere?
Liliom: No one is talking to you.
Marie: You asked us--why we----
Liliom: Will you keep your mouth shut?
Liliom: What do you suppose I want with two of you?
Liliom: I meant that one of you was to wait.
Liliom: The other can go home.
Marie: All right.
Julie: All right.
Julie: [_Neither starts to go._] LILIOM One of you goes home.
Julie: [_To MARIE._] Where do you work?
Marie: At the Breier's, Damjanovitsch Street, Number 20.
Liliom: And you?
Julie: I work there, too.
Liliom: Well, one of you goes home.
Liliom: Which of you wants to stay?
Liliom: [_There is no answer._] Come on, speak up, which of you stays?
[_Officiously._]
Marie: She'll lose her job if she stays.
Liliom: Who will?
Marie: Julie.
Marie: She has to be back by seven o'clock.
Liliom: Is that true?
Liliom: Will they discharge you if you're not back on time?
Julie: Yes.
Liliom: Well, wasn't I discharged?
Julie: Yes--you were discharged, too.
Marie: Julie, shall I go?
Julie: I--can't tell you what to do.
Marie: All right--stay if you like.
Liliom: You'll be discharged if you do?
Marie: Shall I go, Julie?
[_Embarrassed._]
Julie: Why do you keep asking me that?
Marie: You know best what to do.
[_Profoundly moved; slowly._]
Julie: It's all right, Marie, you can go home.
[_Exits reluctantly, but comes back, and says uncertainly._]
Marie: Good-night.
[_She waits a moment to see if JULIE will follow her.
JULIE does not move.
MARIE exits.
Meantime it has grown quite dark.
During the following scene the gas-lamps far in the distance are lighted one by one.
LILIOM and JULIE sit on the bench.
From afar, very faintly, comes the music of a calliope.
But the music is intermittently heard; now it breaks off, now it resumes again, as if it came down on a fitful wind.
Blending with it are the sounds of human voices, now loud, now soft; the blare of a toy trumpet; the confused noises of the show-booths.
It grows progressively darker until the end of the scene.
There is no moonlight.
The spring irridescence glows in the deep blue sky._]
Liliom: Now we're both discharged.
[_She does not answer.
From now on they speak gradually lower and lower until the end of the scene, which is played almost in whispers.
Liliom: Whistles softly, then._] Have you had your supper?
Julie: No.
Liliom: Want to go eat something at the Garden?
Julie: No.
Liliom: Anywhere else?
Julie: No.
[_Whistles softly, then._]
Liliom: You don't come to this park very often, do you?
Liliom: I've only seen you three times.
Liliom: Been here oftener than that?
Julie: Oh, yes.
Liliom: Did you see me?
Julie: Yes.
Liliom: And did you know I was Liliom?
Julie: They told me.
[_Whistles softly, then._]
Liliom: Have you got a sweetheart?
Julie: No.
Liliom: Don't lie to me.
Julie: I haven't.
Julie: If I had, I'd tell you.
Julie: I've never had one.
Liliom: What an awful liar you are.
Liliom: I've got a good mind to go away and leave you here.
Julie: I've never had one.
Liliom: Tell that to someone else.
[_Reproachfully._]
Julie: Why do you insist I have?
Liliom: Because you stayed here with me the first time I asked you to.
Liliom: You know your way around, you do.
Julie: No, I don't, Mister Liliom.

Liliom: I suppose you'll tell me you don't know why you're sitting here--like this, in the dark, alone with me--You wouldn't 'a' stayed so quick, if you hadn't done it before--with some soldier, maybe.
Liliom: This isn't the first time.
Liliom: You wouldn't have been so ready to stay if it was--what _did_ you stay for, anyhow?
Julie: So you wouldn't be left alone.
Liliom: Alone!
Liliom: God, you're dumb!
Liliom: I don't need to be alone.
Liliom: I can have all the girls I want.
Liliom: Not only servant girls like you, but cooks and governesses, even French girls.
Liliom: I could have twenty of them if I wanted to.
Julie: I know, Mister Liliom.
Liliom: What do you know?
Julie: That all the girls are in love with you.
Julie: But that's not why _I_ stayed.
Julie: I stayed because you've been so good to me.
Liliom: Well, then you can go home.
Julie: I don't want to go home now.
Liliom: And what if I go away and leave you sitting here?
Julie: If you did, I wouldn't go home.
Liliom: Do you know what you remind me of?

Liliom: A sweetheart I had once--I'll tell you how I met her---- One night, at closing time, we had put out the lights in the carousel, and just as I was---- [_He is interrupted by the entrance of two plainclothes POLICEMEN.
They take their stations on either side of the bench.
They are police, searching the park for vagabonds._]
Liliom: FIRST POLICEMAN What are you doing there?
Liliom: Stand up when you're spoken to!
Liliom: [_He taps LILIOM imperatively on the shoulder._] FIRST POLICEMAN What's your name?
Liliom: Andreas Zavoczki.
Liliom: [_JULIE begins to weep softly._] SECOND POLICEMAN Stop your bawling.
Liliom: We're not goin' to eat you.
Liliom: We are only making our rounds.
Liliom: FIRST POLICEMAN See that he doesn't get away.
Liliom: [_THE SECOND POLICEMAN steps closer to LILIOM._] What's your business?
Liliom: Barker and bouncer.
Liliom: SECOND POLICEMAN They call him Liliom, Chief.
Liliom: We've had him up a couple of times.
Liliom: FIRST POLICEMAN So that's who you are!
Liliom: Who do you work for now?
Liliom: I work for the widow Muskat.
Liliom: What are you hanging around here for?
Liliom: We're just sitting here--me and this girl.
Liliom: FIRST POLICEMAN Your sweetheart?
Liliom: FIRST POLICEMAN [_To JULIE._] And who are you?
Julie: Julie Zeller.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Servant girl?
Julie: Maid of All Work for Mister Georg Breier, Number Twenty Damjanovitsch Street.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Show your hands.
Julie: SECOND POLICEMAN [_After examining JULIE'S hand._] Servant girl.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Why aren't you at home?
Julie: What are you doing out here with him?
Julie: This is my day out, sir.
Julie: It would be better for you if you didn't spend it sitting around with a fellow like this.
Julie: They'll be disappearing in the bushes as soon as we turn our backs.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN He's only after your money.
Julie: We know this fine fellow.
Julie: He picks up you silly servant girls and takes what money you have.
Julie: Tomorrow you'll probably be coming around to report him.
Julie: If you do, I'll throw you out.
Julie: I haven't any money, sir.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Do you hear that, Liliom?
Liliom: I'm not looking for her money.
Liliom: SECOND POLICEMAN [_Nudging him warningly._] Keep your mouth shut.
Liliom: It is my duty to warn you, my child, what kind of company you're in.
Liliom: He makes a specialty of servant girls.
Liliom: That's why he works in a carousel.
Liliom: He gets hold of a girl, promises to marry her, then he takes her money and her ring.
Julie: But I haven't got a ring.
Julie: You're not to talk unless you're asked a question.
Julie: You be thankful that I'm warning you.
Julie: It's nothing to me what you do.
Julie: I'm not your father, thank God.
Julie: But I'm telling you what kind of a fellow he is.
Julie: By tomorrow morning you'll be coming around to us to report him.
Julie: Now you be sensible and go home.
Julie: You needn't be afraid of him.
Julie: This officer will take you home if you're afraid.
Julie: Do I _have_ to go?
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN No, you don't _have_ to go.
Julie: Then I'll stay, sir.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Well, you've been warned.
Julie: Yes, sir.
Julie: Thank you, sir.
Julie: FIRST POLICEMAN Come on, Berkovics.
[_The POLICEMEN exit.
JULIE and LILIOM sit on the bench again.
There is a brief pause._]
Julie: Well, and what then?
[_Fails to understand._]
Liliom: Huh?
Julie: You were beginning to tell me a story.
Julie: Yes, about a sweetheart.
Julie: You said, one night, just as they were putting out the lights of the carousel---- That's as far as you got.

Liliom: Oh, yes, yes, just as the lights were going out, someone came along--a little girl with a big shawl--you know---- She came--eh--from---- Say--tell me--ain't you--that is, ain't you at all--afraid of me?
Liliom: The officer told you what kind of a fellow I am--and that I'd take your money away from you---JULIE You couldn't take it away--I haven't got any.
Liliom: But if I had--I'd--I'd give it to you--I'd give it all to you.
Liliom: You would?
Julie: If you asked me for it.
Liliom: Have you ever had a fellow you gave money to?
Julie: No.
Liliom: Haven't you ever had a sweetheart?
Julie: No.
Liliom: Someone you used to go walking with.
Liliom: You've had one like that?
Julie: Yes.
Liliom: A soldier?
Julie: He came from the same village I did.
Liliom: That's what all the soldiers say.
Liliom: Where _do_ you come from, anyway?
Julie: Not far from here.
Julie: [_There is a pause._] LILIOM Were you in love with him?
Julie: Why do you keep asking me that all the time, Mister Liliom?
Julie: I wasn't in love with him.
Julie: We only went walking together.
Liliom: Where did you walk?
Julie: In the park.
Liliom: And your virtue?
Liliom: Where did you lose that?
Julie: I haven't got any virtue.
Liliom: Well, you had once.
Julie: No, I never had.
Julie: I'm a respectable girl.
Liliom: Yes, but you gave the soldier something.
Julie: Why do you question me like that, Mister Liliom?
Liliom: Did you give him something?
Julie: You have to.
Julie: But I didn't love him.
Liliom: Do you love me?
Julie: No, Mister Liliom.
Liliom: Then why do you stay here with me?
Julie: Um--nothing.
[_There is a pause.
The music from afar is plainly heard._]
Liliom: Want to dance?
Julie: No.
Julie: I have to be very careful.
Liliom: Of what?
Julie: My--character.
Liliom: Why?
Julie: Because I'm never going to marry.
Julie: If I was going to marry, it would be different.
Julie: Then I wouldn't need to worry so much about my character.
Julie: It doesn't make any difference if you're married.
Julie: But I shan't marry--and that's why I've got to take care to be a respectable girl.
Liliom: Suppose I were to say to you--I'll marry you.
Julie: You?
Liliom: That frightens you, doesn't it?
Liliom: You're thinking of what the officer said and you're afraid.
Julie: No, I'm not, Mister Liliom.
Julie: I don't pay any attention to what he said.
Liliom: But you wouldn't dare to marry anyone like me, would you?
Julie: I know that--that--if I loved anyone--it wouldn't make any difference to me what he--even if I died for it.
Liliom: But you wouldn't marry a rough guy like me--that is,--eh--if you loved me---JULIE Yes, I would--if I loved you, Mister Liliom.
Liliom: [_There is a pause._] LILIOM [_Whispers._] Well,--you just said--didn't you?--that you don't love me.
Liliom: Well, why don't you go home then?
Julie: It's too late now, they'd all be asleep.
Liliom: Locked out?
Julie: Certainly.
Julie: [_They are silent a while._] LILIOM I think--that even a low-down good-for-nothing--can make a man of himself.
Julie: Certainly.
[_They are silent again.
Julie: A lamp-lighter crosses the stage, lights the lamp over the bench, and exits._] LILIOM Are you hungry?
Julie: No.
Julie: [_Another pause._] LILIOM Suppose--you had some money--and I took it from you?
Julie: Then you could take it, that's all.
[_After another brief silence._]
Liliom: All I have to do--is go back to her--that Muskat woman--she'll be glad to get me back--then I'd be earning my wages again.
[_She is silent.
The twilight folds darker about them._]
[_Very softly._]
Julie: Don't go back--to her---- [_Pause._]
Liliom: There are a lot of acacia trees around here.
Liliom: [_Pause._] JULIE Don't go back to her---- [_Pause._] LILIOM She'd take me back the minute I asked her.
Liliom: I know why--she knows, too---- [_Pause._]
Julie: I can smell them, too--acacia blossoms---- [_There is a pause.
Some blossoms drift down from the tree-top to the bench.
LILIOM picks one up and smells it._]
Liliom: White acacias!
[_After a brief pause._]
Julie: The wind brings them down.
[_They are silent.
There is a long pause before_]
SCENE--_A photographer's "studio," operated by the HOLLUNDERS, on the fringe of the park.
It is a dilapidated hovel.
The general entrance is Back Left.
Back Right there is a window with a sofa before it.

The outlook is on the amusement park with perhaps a small Ferris-wheel or the scaffolding of a "scenic-railway" in the background._ _The door to the kitchen is up Left and a black-curtained entrance to the dark room is down Left.
Just in front of the dark room stands the camera on its tripod.
Against the back wall, between the door and window, stands the inevitable photographer's background-screen, ready to be wheeled into place._ _It is forenoon.
When the curtain rises, MARIE and JULIE are discovered._
Marie: And _he_ beat up Hollinger?
Julie: Yes, he gave him an awful licking.
Marie: But Hollinger is bigger than he is.
Julie: He licked him just the same.
Julie: It isn't size that counts, you know, it's cleverness.
Julie: And Liliom's awful quick.
Marie: And then he was arrested?
Julie: Yes, they arrested him, but they let him go the next day.
Julie: That makes twice in the two months we've been living here that Liliom's been arrested and let go again.
Marie: Why do they let him go?
Julie: Because he is innocent.

Julie: [_MOTHER HOLLUNDER, a very old woman, sharp-tongued, but in reality quite warm-hearted beneath her formidable exterior, enters at back carrying a few sticks of firewood, and scolding, half to herself._] MOTHER HOLLUNDER Always wanting something, but never willing to work for it.
Julie: He won't work, and he won't steal, but he'll use up a poor old widow's last bit of firewood.
Julie: He'll do that cheerfully enough!
Julie: A big, strong lout like that lying around all day resting his lazy bones!
Julie: He ought to be ashamed to look decent people in the face.
Julie: I'm sorry, Mother Hollunder. . . .
Julie: MOTHER HOLLUNDER Sorry!
Julie: Better be sorry the lazy good-for-nothing ain't in jail where he belongs instead of in the way of honest, hard-working people.
Julie: [_She exits into the kitchen._] MARIE Who's that?
Julie: Mrs. Hollunder--my aunt.
Julie: This is her [_with a sweeping gesture that takes in the camera, dark room and screen_] studio.
Julie: She lets us live here for nothing.
Marie: What's she fetching the wood for?
Julie: She brings us everything we need.
Julie: If it weren't for her I don't know what would become of us.
Julie: She's a good-hearted soul even if her tongue is sharp.
Julie: [_There is a pause._] MARIE [_Shyly._] Do you know--I've found out.
Julie: He's not a soldier.
Julie: Do you still see him?
Marie: Oh, yes.
Julie: Often?
Marie: Very often.
Marie: He's asked me----
Julie: To marry you?
Marie: To marry me.
Julie: You see--that proves he isn't a soldier.
Julie: [_There is another pause._] MARIE [_Abashed, yet a bit boastfully._] Do you know what I'm doing--I'm flirting with him.
Julie: Flirting?
Marie: Yes.
Marie: He asks me to go to the park--and I say I can't go.
Marie: Then he coaxes me, and promises me a new scarf for my head if I go.
Marie: But I don't go--even then. . . .
Marie: So then he walks all the way home with me--and I bid him good-night at the door.
Julie: Is that what you call flirting?
Marie: Um-hm!
Marie: It's sinful, but it's so _thrilling._
Julie: Do you ever quarrel?
[_Grandly._]
Marie: Only when our Passionate Love surges up.
Julie: Your passionate love?
Marie: Yes. . . .
Marie: He takes my hand and we walk along together.
Marie: Then he wants to swing hands, but I won't let him.
Marie: I say: "Don't swing my hand"; and he says, "Don't be so stubborn."
Marie: And then he tries to swing my hand again, but still I don't let him.
Marie: And for a long time I don't let him--until in the end I let him.
Marie: Then we walk along swinging hands--up and down, up and down--just like this. _That_ is Passionate Love.
Marie: It's sinful, but it's awfully _thrilling._
Julie: You're happy, aren't you?
Marie: Happier than--anything---- But the most beautiful thing on earth is Ideal Love.
Julie: What kind is that?
Marie: Daylight comes about three in the morning this time of the year.
Marie: When we've been up that long we're all through with flirting and Passionate Love--and then our Ideal Love comes to the surface.
Marie: It comes like this: I'll be sitting on the bench and Wolf, he holds my hand tight--and he puts his cheek against my cheek and we don't talk . . . we just sit there very quiet. . . .
Marie: And after a while he gets sleepy, and his head sinks down, and he falls asleep . . . but even in his sleep he holds tight to my hand.
Marie: And I--I sit perfectly still just looking around me and taking long, deep breaths--for by that time it's morning and the trees and flowers are fresh with dew.
Marie: But Wolf doesn't smell anything because he's so fast asleep.
Marie: And I get awfully sleepy myself, but I don't sleep.
Marie: And we sit like that for a long time.
Marie: That is Ideal Love---- [_There is a long pause._]
[_Regretfully; uneasily._]
Julie: He went out last night and he hasn't come home yet.
Marie: Here are sixteen Kreuzer.
Marie: It was supposed to be carfare to take my young lady to the conservatory--eight there and eight back--but I made her walk.
Marie: Here--save it with the rest.
Julie: This makes three gulden, forty-six.
Marie: Three gulden, forty-six.
Julie: He won't work at all.
Marie: Too lazy?
Julie: No.
Julie: He never learned a trade, you see, and he can't just go and be a day-laborer--so he just does nothing.
Marie: That ain't right.
Julie: No.
Julie: Have the Breiers got a new maid yet?
Marie: They've had three since you left.
Marie: You know, Wolf's going to take a new job.
Marie: He's going to work for the city.
Marie: He'll get rent free, too.
Julie: He won't go back to work at the carousel either.
Julie: I ask him why, but he won't tell me---- Last Monday he hit me.
Marie: Did you hit him back?
Julie: No.
Marie: Why don't you leave him?
Julie: I don't want to.
Marie: I would.
Marie: I'd leave him.
Marie: [_There is a strained silence._] MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Enters, carrying a pot of water; muttering aloud._] He can play cards, all right.
Marie: He can fight, too; and take money from poor servant girls.
Marie: And the police turn their heads the other way---- The carpenter was here.
Julie: Is that water for the soup?
Julie: MOTHER HOLLUNDER The carpenter was here.
Julie: There's a _man_ for you!
Julie: Dark, handsome, lots of hair, a respectable widower with two children--and money, and a good paying business.
[_To MARIE._]
Julie: It's three gulden sixty-six, not forty-six.
Marie: Yes, that's what I make it--sixty-six.
Marie: He wants to take her out of this and marry her.
Marie: This is the fifth time he's been here.
Marie: He has two children, but----
Julie: Please don't bother, Aunt Hollunder, I'll get the water myself.
Julie: MOTHER HOLLUNDER He's waiting outside now.
Julie: Send him away.
Julie: He'll only come back again--and first thing you know that vagabond will get jealous and there'll be a fight.
Julie: [_Goes out, muttering._] Oh, he's ready enough to fight, he is.
Julie: Strike a poor little girl like that!
Julie: Ought to be ashamed of himself!
Julie: And the police just let him go on doing as he pleases.
Julie: [_Still scolding, she exits at back._] MARIE A carpenter wants to marry you?
Julie: Yes.
Marie: Why don't you?
Julie: Because----
Marie: Liliom doesn't support you, and he beats you--he thinks he can do whatever he likes just because he's Liliom.
Marie: He's a bad one.
Julie: He's not really bad.
Marie: That night you sat on the bench together--he was gentle then.
Julie: Yes, he was gentle.
Marie: And afterwards he got wild again.
Julie: Afterwards he got wild--sometimes.
Julie: But that night on the bench . . . he was gentle.
Julie: He's gentle now, sometimes, very gentle.
Julie: After supper, when he stands there and listens to the music of the carousel, something comes over him--and he is gentle.
Marie: Does he say anything?
Julie: He doesn't say anything.
Julie: He gets thoughtful and very quiet, and his big eyes stare straight ahead of him.
Marie: Into your eyes?
Julie: Not exactly.
Julie: He's unhappy because he isn't working.
Julie: That's really why he hit me on Monday.
Marie: That's a fine reason for hitting you!
Marie: Beats his wife because he isn't working, the ruffian!
Julie: It preys on his mind----
Marie: Did he hurt you?
[_Very eagerly._]
Julie: Oh, no.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT [_Enters haughtily._] Good morning.
Julie: Is Liliom home?
Julie: No.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT Gone out?
Julie: He hasn't come home yet.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT I'll wait for him.
Julie: [_She sits down._] MARIE You've got a lot of gall--to come here.
Julie: Are you the lady of the house, my dear?
Julie: Better look out or you'll get a slap in the mouth.
Marie: How dare you set foot in Julie's house?
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT [_To JULIE._] Pay no attention to her, my child.
Marie: You know what brings me here.
Marie: That vagabond, that good-for-nothing, I've come to give him his bread and butter back.
Marie: He's not dependent on you for his bread.
Marie: MRS. MUSKAT [_To JULIE._] Just ignore her, my child.
Marie: She's just ignorant.
[_Going._]
Marie: Good-bye.
Julie: Good-bye.
[_In the doorway, calling back._]
Marie: Sixty-six.
Julie: Yes, sixty-six.
Marie: Good-bye.
[_She exits.
JULIE starts to go toward the kitchen._]
Marie: I paid him a krone a day, and on Sunday a gulden.
Marie: And he got all the beer and cigars he wanted from the customers.
Marie: [_JULIE pauses on the threshold, but does not answer._] And he'd rather starve than beg my pardon.
Marie: Well, I don't insist on that.
Marie: I'll take him back without it.
Marie: [_JULIE does not answer._] The fact is the people ask for him--and, you see, I've got to consider business first.
Marie: It's nothing to me if he starves.
Marie: I wouldn't be here at all, if it wasn't for business---- [_She pauses, for LILIOM and FICSUR have entered._] JULIE Mrs. Muskat is here.
Liliom: I see she is.
Julie: You might say good-morning.
Liliom: What for?
Liliom: And what do _you_ want, anyhow?
Julie: I don't want anything.
Liliom: Then keep your mouth shut.
Liliom: Next thing you'll be starting to nag again about my being out all night and out of work and living on your relations---JULIE I'm not saying anything.
Liliom: But it's all on the tip of your tongue--I know you--now don't start or you'll get another.
[_He paces angrily up and down.
They are all a bit afraid of him, and shrink and look away as he passes them.

Liliom: FICSUR shambles from place to place, his eyes cast down as if he were searching for something on the floor._] MRS. MUSKAT [_Suddenly, to FICSUR._] You're always dragging him out to play cards and drink with you.
Liliom: I'll have you locked up, I will.
Ficsur: I don't want to talk to you.
Ficsur: You're too common.
[_He goes out by the door at back and lingers there in plain view.
There is a pause._]
Julie: Mrs. Muskat is here.
Liliom: Well, why doesn't she open her mouth, if she has anything to say?
Liliom: Why do you go around with this man Ficsur?
Liliom: He'll get you mixed up in one of his robberies first thing you know.
Liliom: What's it to you who I go with?
Liliom: I do what I please.
Liliom: What do you want?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT You know what I want.
Liliom: No, I don't.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT What do you suppose I want?
Liliom: Think I've come just to pay a social call?
Liliom: Do I owe you anything?
Liliom: Yes, you do--but that's not what I came for.
Liliom: You're a fine one to come to for money!
Liliom: You earn so much these days!
Liliom: You know very well what I'm here for.
Liliom: You've got Hollinger at the carousel, haven't you?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Sure I have.
Liliom: Well, what else do you want?
Liliom: He's as good as I am.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT You're quite right, my boy.
Liliom: He's every bit as good as you are.
Liliom: I'd not dream of letting him go.
Liliom: But one isn't enough any more.
Liliom: There's work enough for two----
Liliom: One was enough when _I_ was there.
Liliom: Well, I might let Hollinger go----
Liliom: Why let him go, if he's so good?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Shrugs her shoulders._] Yes, he's good.
Liliom: [_Not once until now has she looked at LILIOM._] LILIOM [_To JULIE._] Ask your aunt if I can have a cup of coffee.
Liliom: [_JULIE exits into the kitchen._] So Hollinger is good, is he?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Crosses to him and looks him, in the face._] Why don't you stay home and sleep at night?
Liliom: You're a sight to look at.
Liliom: He's good, is he?
Liliom: Push your hair back from your forehead.
Liliom: Let my hair be.
Liliom: It's nothing to you.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT All right.
Liliom: But if I'd told you to let it hang down over your eyes you'd have pushed it back--I hear you've been beating her, this--this---LILIOM None of your business.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT You're a fine fellow!
Liliom: Beating a skinny little thing like that!
Liliom: If you're tired of her, leave her, but there's no use beating the poor---LILIOM Leave her, eh?
Liliom: You'd like that, wouldn't you?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Don't flatter yourself.
Liliom: [_Quite embarrassed._] Serves me right, too.
Liliom: If I had any sense I wouldn't have run after you---- My God, the things one must do for the sake of business!
Liliom: If I could only sell the carousel I wouldn't be sitting here. . . .
Liliom: Come, Liliom, if you have any sense, you'll come back.
Liliom: I'll pay you well.
Liliom: The carousel is crowded just the same . . . _without me?_ MRS. MUSKAT Crowded, yes--but it's not the same.
Liliom: Then you admit that you _do_ miss me.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Miss you?
Liliom: Not I. But the silly girls miss you.
Liliom: They're always asking for you.
Liliom: Well, are you going to be sensible and come back?
Liliom: And leave--her?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT You beat her, don't you?
Liliom: No, I don't beat her.
Liliom: What's all this damn fool talk about beating her?
Liliom: I hit her once--that was all--and now the whole city seems to be talking about it.
Liliom: You don't call that beating her, do you?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT All right, all right.
Liliom: I take it back.
Liliom: I don't want to get mixed up in it.
Liliom: Beating her!
Liliom: As if I'd beat her----
Liliom: I can't make out why you're so concerned about her.
Liliom: You've been married to her two months--it's plain to see that you're sick of it--and out there is the carousel--and the show booths--and money--and you'd throw it all away.
Liliom: For what?
Liliom: Heavens, how can anyone be such a fool?
Liliom: [_Looks at him appraisingly._] Where have you been all night?
Liliom: You look awful.
Liliom: It's no business of yours.
Liliom: You never used to look like that.
Liliom: This life is telling on you.
Liliom: [_Pauses._] Do you know--I've got a new organ.
[_Softly._]
Liliom: I know.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT How did you know?
Liliom: You can hear it--from here.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT It's a good one, eh?
[_Wistfully._]
Liliom: Very good.
Liliom: Fine. It roars and snorts--so fine.
Liliom: You should hear it close by--it's heavenly.
Liliom: Even the carousel seems to know . . . it goes quicker.
Liliom: I got rid of those two horses--you know, the ones with the broken ears?
Liliom: What have you put in their place?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Guess.
Liliom: Zebras?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT No--an automobile.
[_Transported._]
Liliom: An automobile----
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Yes.
Liliom: If you've got any sense you'll come back.
Liliom: What good are you doing here?
Liliom: Out there is your _art_, the only thing you're fit for.
Liliom: You are an artist, not a respectable married man.
Liliom: _Leave_ her--this little----
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT She'll be better off.
Liliom: She'll go back and be a servant girl again.
Liliom: As for you--you're an artist and you belong among artists.
Liliom: All the beer you want, cigars, a krone a day and a gulden on Sunday, and the girls, Liliom, the girls--I've always treated you right, haven't I?
Liliom: I bought you a watch, and----
Liliom: She's not that kind.
Liliom: She'd never be a servant girl again.
Liliom: I suppose you think she'd kill herself.
Liliom: Don't worry.

Liliom: Heavens, if every girl was to commit suicide just because her---- [_Finishes with a gesture._] LILIOM [_Stares at her a moment, considering, then with sudden, smiling animation._] So the people don't like Hollinger?
Liliom: You know very well they don't, you rascal.
Liliom: Well----
Liliom: You've always been happy at the carousel.
Liliom: It's a great life--pretty girls and beer and cigars and music--a great life and an easy one.
Liliom: I'll tell you what--come back and I'll give you a ring that used to belong to my dear departed husband.
Liliom: Well, will you come?
Liliom: She's not that kind.
Liliom: She'd never be a servant girl again.
Liliom: But--but--for my part--if I decide--that needn't make any difference.
Liliom: I can go on living with her even if I do go back to my art---MRS. MUSKAT My God!
Liliom: What's the matter?
Liliom: Who ever heard of a married man--I suppose you think all girls would be pleased to know that you were running home to your wife every night.
Liliom: It's ridiculous!
Liliom: When the people found out they'd laugh themselves sick----
Liliom: I know what you want.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Refuses to meet his gaze._] You flatter yourself.
Liliom: You'll give me that ring, too?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Pushes the hair back from his forehead._] Yes.
Liliom: I'm not happy in this house.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT [_Still stroking his hair._] Nobody takes care of you.
[_They are silent.
JULIE enters, carrying a cup of coffee.
MRS. MUSKAT removes her hand from LILIOM'S head.
There is a pause._]
Liliom: Do you want anything?
Julie: No.
[_There is a pause.
She exits slowly into the kitchen._]
Julie: The old woman says there is a carpenter, a widower, who---LILIOM I know--I know---JULIE [_Reëntering._] Liliom, before I forget, I have something to tell you.
Liliom: All right.
Julie: I've been wanting to tell you--in fact, I was going to tell you yesterday---LILIOM Go ahead.
Julie: But I must tell you alone--if you'll come in--it will only take a minute.
Liliom: Don't you see I'm busy now?
Liliom: Here I am talking business and you interrupt with----
Julie: It'll only take a minute.
Liliom: Get out of here, or----
Julie: But I tell you it will only take a minute----
Liliom: Will you get out of here?
[_Courageously._]
Julie: No.
[_Rising._]
Liliom: What's that!
Julie: No.
Julie: MRS. MUSKAT [_Rises, too._] Now don't start fighting.
Julie: I'll go out and look at the photographs in the show-case a while and come back later for your answer.
Julie: [_She exits at back._] JULIE You can hit me again if you like--don't look at me like that.
Julie: I'm not afraid of you. . . .
Julie: I'm not afraid of anyone.
Julie: I told you I had something to tell you.
Liliom: Well, out with it--quick.
Julie: I can't tell you so quick.
Julie: Why don't you drink your coffee?
Liliom: Is that what you wanted to tell me?
Julie: No.
Julie: By the time you've drunk your coffee I'll have told you.
[_Gets the coffee and sips it._]
Liliom: Well?
Julie: Yesterday my head ached--and you asked me----
Liliom: Yes----
Julie: Well--you see--that's what it is----
Liliom: Are you sick?
Julie: No. . . .
Julie: But you wanted to know what my headaches came from--and you said I seemed--changed.
Liliom: Did I?
Liliom: I guess I meant the carpenter.
Julie: I've been--what?
Julie: The carpenter?

Julie: No. It's something entirely different--it's awful hard to tell--but you'll have to know sooner or later--I'm not a bit--scared--because it's a perfectly natural thing---LILIOM [_Puts the coffee cup on the table._] What?
Julie: When--when a man and woman--live together----
Liliom: Yes.
Julie: I'm going to have a baby.
[_She exits swiftly at back.
There is a pause.
FICSUR appears at the open window and looks in._]
Liliom: Ficsur!
Liliom: [_FICSUR sticks his head in._] Say, Ficsur,--Julie is going to have a baby.
Ficsur: Yes?
Ficsur: What of it?
Liliom: Nothing.
Liliom: [_Suddenly._] Get out of here.
[_FICSUR'S head is quickly withdrawn.
MRS. MUSKAT reënters._]
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Has she gone?
Liliom: Yes.
Liliom: I might as well give you ten kronen in advance.
[_Opens her purse.
Liliom: LILIOM takes up his coffee cup._] Here you are.
[_She proffers some coins.
Liliom: LILIOM ignores her._] Why don't you take it?
[_Very nonchalantly, his cup poised ready to drink._]
Liliom: Go home, Mrs. Muskat.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT What's the matter with you?
Liliom: Go home [_sips his coffee_] and let me finish my coffee in peace.
Liliom: Don't you see I'm at breakfast?
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Have you gone crazy?
Liliom: Will you get out of here?
Liliom: [_Turns to her threateningly._] MRS. MUSKAT [_Restoring the coins to her purse._] I'll never speak to you again as long as you live.
Liliom: That worries me a lot.
Liliom: MRS. MUSKAT Good-bye!
Liliom: Good-bye.
Liliom: [_As she exits, he calls._] Ficsur!
Liliom: [_FICSUR enters._] Tell me, Ficsur.
Liliom: You said you knew a way to get a whole lot of money---FICSUR Sure I do.
Liliom: How much?
Ficsur: More than you ever had in your life before.
Ficsur: You leave it to an old hand like me.

Ficsur: MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Enters from the kitchen._] In the morning he must have his coffee, and at noon his soup, and in the evening coffee again--and plenty of firewood--and I'm expected to furnish it all.
Ficsur: Give me back my cup and saucer.
[_The show booths of the amusement-park have opened for business.
Ficsur: The familiar noises begin to sound; clear above them all, but far in the distance, sounds the organ of the carousel._] LILIOM Now, Aunt Hollunder.

Ficsur: [_From now until the fall of the curtain it is apparent that the sound of the organ makes him more and more uneasy._] MOTHER HOLLUNDER And you, you vagabond, get out of here this minute or I'll call my son---FICSUR I have nothing to do with the likes of him.
Ficsur: He's too common.
Ficsur: [_But he slinks out at back._] LILIOM Aunt Hollunder!
Ficsur: MOTHER HOLLUNDER What now?
Liliom: When your son was born--when you brought him into the world---MOTHER HOLLUNDER Well?
Liliom: Nothing.
Liliom: MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Muttering as she exits._] Sleep it off, you good-for-nothing lout.
Liliom: Drink and play cards all night long--that's all you know how to do--and take the bread out of poor people's mouths--you can do that, too.
Liliom: [_She exits._] LILIOM Ficsur!
[_At the window._]
Ficsur: Julie's going to have a baby.
Ficsur: You told me before.
Liliom: This scheme--about the cashier of the leather factory--there's money in it---FICSUR Lots of money--but--it takes two to pull it off.
[_Meditatively._]
Liliom: Yes.
Liliom: [_Uneasily._] All right, Ficsur.
Liliom: Go away--and come back later.
[_FICSUR vanishes.
The organ in the distant carousel drones incessantly.
Liliom: LILIOM listens a while, then goes to the door and calls._] LILIOM Aunt Hollunder!
Liliom: [_With naïve joy._] Julie's going to have a baby.
[_Then he goes to the window, jumps on the sofa, looks out.
Liliom: Suddenly, in a voice that overtops the droning of the organ, he shouts as if addressing the far-off carousel._] I'm going to be a father.
[_Enters from the kitchen._]
Julie: Liliom!
Julie: What's the matter?
Julie: What's happened?
[_Coming down from the sofa._]
Liliom: Nothing.
[_Throws himself on the sofa, buries his face in the cushion.
JULIE watches him a moment, comes over to him and covers him with a shawl.
Liliom: Then she goes on tip-toe to the door at back and remains standing in the doorway, looking out and listening to the droning of the organ._] THE CURTAIN FALLS
SCENE--_The setting is the same, later that afternoon.
LILIOM is sitting opposite FICSUR, who is teaching him a song.
JULIE hovers in the background, engaged in some household task._
Ficsur: Listen now.
Ficsur: Here's the third verse.
Ficsur: [_Sings hoarsely._] "Look out, look out, my pretty lad.

Ficsur: The damn police are on your trail; The nicest girl you ever had Has now commenced to weep and wail: Look out here comes the damn police, The damn police, The damn police, Look out here comes the damn police, They'll get you every time."
[_Sings._]
Liliom: "Look out, look out, my pretty lad.
Liliom: The damn police----"
Liliom: FICSUR, LILIOM [_Sing together._]
Liliom: "Are on your trail The nicest girl you ever had Has now commenced to weep and wail."
[_Alone._]

Liliom: "Look out here comes the damn police, The damn police, The damn police----" [_JULIE, troubled and uneasy, looks from one to the other, then exits into the kitchen._] FICSUR [_When she has gone, comes quickly over to LILIOM and speaks furtively._] As you go down Franzen Street you come to the railroad embankment.
Liliom: Beyond that--all the way to the leather factory--there's not a thing in sight, not even a watchman's hut.
Liliom: And does he always come that way?
Ficsur: Yes.
Ficsur: Not along the embankment, but down below along the path across the fields.
Ficsur: Since last year he's been going alone.
Ficsur: Before that he always used to have someone with him.
Liliom: Every Saturday?
Ficsur: Every Saturday.
Liliom: And the money?
Liliom: Where does he keep it?
Ficsur: In a leather bag.
Ficsur: The whole week's pay for the workmen at the factory.
Liliom: Much?
Ficsur: Sixteen thousand kronen.
Ficsur: Quite a haul, what?
Liliom: What's his name?
Ficsur: Linzman.
Ficsur: He's a Jew.
Liliom: The cashier?
Ficsur: Yes--but when he gets a knife between his ribs--or if I smash his skull for him--he won't be a cashier any more.
Liliom: Does he have to be killed?
Ficsur: No, he doesn't _have_ to be.
Ficsur: He can give up the money _without_ being killed--but most of these cashiers are peculiar--they'd rather be killed.
[_JULIE reënters, pretends to get something on the other side of the room, then exits at back.
During the ensuing dialogue she keeps coming in and out in the same way, showing plainly that she is suspicious and anxious.
She attempts to overhear what they are saying and, in spite of their caution, does catch a word here and there, which adds to her disquiet.
FICSUR, catching sight of her, abruptly changes the conversation._]
Ficsur: And the next verse is:
Ficsur: "And when you're in the prison cell They'll feed you bread and water."
Ficsur: FICSUR AND LILIOM [_Sing together._]
Ficsur: "They'll make your little sweetheart tell Them all the things you brought her.
Ficsur: Look out here comes the damn police, The damn police, The damn police.
Ficsur: Look out here comes the damn police They'll get you every time."
[_Sings alone._]
Liliom: "And when you're in the prison cell They'll feed you bread and water----" [_Breaks off as JULIE exits._] And when it's done, do we start right off for America?
Liliom: What then?
Ficsur: We bury the money for six months.
Ficsur: That's the usual time.
Ficsur: And after the sixth month we dig it up again.
Liliom: And then?
Ficsur: Then you go on living just as usual for six months more--you don't touch a heller of the money.
Liliom: In six months the baby will be born.
Ficsur: Then we'll take the baby with us, too.
Ficsur: Three months before the time you'll go to work so as to be able to say you saved up your wages to get to America.
Liliom: Which of us goes up and talks to him?
Ficsur: One of us talks to him with his mouth and the other talks with his knife.
Ficsur: Depends on which you'd rather do.
Ficsur: I'll tell you what--you talk to him with your mouth.
Liliom: Do you hear that?
Ficsur: What?
Liliom: Outside . . . like the rattle of swords.
[_FICSUR listens.
Liliom: After a pause, LILIOM continues._] What do I say to him?
Ficsur: You say good evening to him and: "Excuse me, sir; can you tell me the time?"
Liliom: And then what?
Ficsur: By that time I'll have stuck him--and then you take _your_ knife---- [_He stops as a POLICEMAN enters at back._] POLICEMAN Good-day!
Ficsur: FICSUR, LILIOM [_In unison._] Good-day!
[_Calling toward the kitchen._]
Ficsur: Hey, photographer, come out. . . .
Ficsur: Here's a customer.
[_There is a pause.
The POLICEMAN waits.
FICSUR sings softly._]
Ficsur: "And when you're in the prison cell They'll feed you bread and water They'll make your little sweetheart tell."
Ficsur: LILIOM, FICSUR [_Sing together, low._]
Ficsur: "Them all the things you brought her.
Ficsur: Look out here comes the----" [_They hum the rest so as not to let the POLICEMAN hear the words "the damn police."
As they sing, MRS. HOLLUNDER and her son enter._]
Ficsur: Do you make cabinet photographs?
Ficsur: YOUNG HOLLUNDER Certainly, sir.
Ficsur: [_Points to a rack of photographs on the wall._] Take your choice, sir.
Ficsur: Would you like one full length?
Ficsur: POLICEMAN Yes, full length.

[_MOTHER HOLLUNDER pushes out the camera while her son poses the POLICEMAN, runs from him to the camera and back again, now altering the pose, now ducking under the black cloth and pushing the camera nearer.
Meanwhile MOTHER HOLLUNDER has fetched a plate from the dark room and thrust it in the camera.
While this is going on,
Ficsur: LILIOM and FICSUR, their heads together, speak in very low tones._] LILIOM Belong around here?
Ficsur: Not around here.
Liliom: Where, then?
Ficsur: Suburban.
Ficsur: [_There is a pause._] LILIOM [_Bursts out suddenly in a rather grotesquely childish and overstrained lament._] O God, what a dirty life I'm leading--God, God!
[_Reassuring him benevolently._]
Ficsur: Over in America it will be better, all right.
Liliom: What's over there?
[_Virtuously._]
Ficsur: Factories . . . industries----
Ficsur: YOUNG HOLLUNDER [_To the POLICEMAN._] Now, quite still, please.
Ficsur: One, two, three.
Ficsur: [_Deftly removes the cover of the lens and in a few seconds restores it._] Thank you.
Ficsur: The picture will be ready in five minutes.
Ficsur: POLICEMAN Good.
Ficsur: I'll come back in five minutes.
Ficsur: How much do I owe you?
Ficsur: YOUNG HOLLUNDER [_With exaggerated deference._] You don't need to pay in advance, Mr. Commissioner.
[_The POLICEMAN salutes condescendingly and exits at back.
MOTHER HOLLUNDER carries the plate into the dark room.
Ficsur: YOUNG HOLLUNDER, after pushing the camera back in place, follows her._] MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Muttering angrily as she passes FICSUR and LILIOM._] You hang around and dirty the whole place up!
Ficsur: Why don't you go take a walk?
Ficsur: Things are going so well with you that you have to sing, eh?
Ficsur: [_Confronting FICSUR suddenly._] Weren't you frightened sick when you saw the policeman?
[_With loathing._]
Ficsur: Go 'way, or I'll step on you.
Ficsur: [_She exits into the dark room._] LILIOM They like Hollinger at the carousel?
Ficsur: I should say they do.
Liliom: Did you see the Muskat woman, too?
Ficsur: Sure.
Ficsur: She takes care of Hollinger's hair.
Liliom: Combs his hair?
Ficsur: She fixes him all up.
Liliom: Let her fix him all she likes.
[_Urging him toward the kitchen door._]
Ficsur: Go on.
Ficsur: Now's your chance.
Liliom: What for?
Ficsur: To get the knife.
Liliom: What knife?
Ficsur: The kitchen knife.
Ficsur: I've got a pocket-knife, but if he shows fight, we'll let him have the big knife.
Liliom: What for?
Liliom: If he gets ugly, I'll bat him one over the head that'll make him squint for the rest of his life.
Ficsur: You've got to have something on you.
Ficsur: You can't slit his throat with a bat over the head.
Liliom: Must his throat be slit?
Ficsur: No, it _mustn't._ But if he asks for it.
Ficsur: [_There is a pause._] You'd like to sail on the big steamer, wouldn't you?
Ficsur: And you want to see the factories over there, don't you?
Ficsur: But you're not willing to inconvenience yourself a little for them.
Liliom: If I take the knife, Julie will see me.
Ficsur: Take it so she won't see you.
[_Advances a few paces toward the kitchen.
The POLICEMAN enters at back.
Liliom: LILIOM knocks on the door of the dark room._] Here's the policeman!
Liliom: MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Coming out._] One minute more, please.
Liliom: Just a minute.
[_She reënters the dark room.
LILIOM hesitates a moment, then exits into the kitchen.
The POLICEMAN scrutinizes FICSUR mockingly.
FICSUR returns his stare, walks a few paces toward him, then deliberately turns his back.
Liliom: Suddenly he wheels around, points at the POLICEMAN and addresses him in a teasing, childish tone._] Christiana Street at the corner of Retti!
Liliom: POLICEMAN [_Amazed, self-conscious._] How do you know that?
Ficsur: I used to practice my profession in that neighborhood.
Ficsur: POLICEMAN What is your profession?
Ficsur: Professor of pianola---- [_The POLICEMAN glares, aware that the man is joking with him, twirls his moustache indignantly.
Ficsur: YOUNG HOLLUNDER comes out of the dark room and gives him the finished pictures._] YOUNG HOLLUNDER Here you are, sir.
[_The POLICEMAN examines the photographs, pays for them, starts to go, stops, glares at FICSUR and exits.
When he is gone, FICSUR goes to the doorway and looks out after him.
YOUNG HOLLUNDER exits.
LILIOM reënters, buttoning his coat._]
[_Turns, sees LILIOM._]
Ficsur: What are you staring at?
Liliom: I'm not staring.
Ficsur: What then are you doing?
Liliom: I'm thinking it over.
[_Comes very close to him._]
Ficsur: Tell me then--what will you say to him?
[_Unsteadily._]
Liliom: I'll say--"Good evening--Excuse me, sir--Can you tell me the time?"
Liliom: And suppose he answers me, what do I say to him?
Ficsur: He won't answer you.
Liliom: Don't you think so?
Liliom: [_Feeling for the knife under LILIOM'S coat._] Where is it?
Liliom: Where did you put it?
[_Stonily._]
Liliom: Left side.
Ficsur: That's right--over your heart.
Ficsur: [_Feels it._] Ah--there it is--there--there's the blade--quite a big fellow, isn't it--ah, here it begins to get narrower.
Ficsur: [_Reaches the tip of the knife._] And here is its eye--that's what it sees with.
[_JULIE enters from the kitchen, passes them slowly, watching them in silent terror, then stops.
Ficsur: FICSUR nudges LILIOM._] Sing, come on, sing!
[_In a quavering voice._]
Liliom: "Look out for the damn police."
[_Joining in, cheerily, loudly, marking time with the swaying of his body._]
Ficsur: "Look out, look out, my pretty lad."
Liliom: "--look out, my pretty lad."
[_JULIE goes out at back.
LILIOM'S glance follows her.
Liliom: When she has gone, he turns to FICSUR._] At night--in my dreams--if his ghost comes back--what will I do then?
Ficsur: His ghost won't never come back.
Liliom: Why not?
Ficsur: A Jew's ghost don't come back.
Liliom: Well then--afterwards----
[_Impatiently._]
Ficsur: What do you mean--afterwards?
Liliom: In the next world--when I come up before the Lord God--what'll I say then?
Ficsur: The likes of you will never come up before Him.
Liliom: Why not?
Ficsur: Have you ever come up before the high court?
Ficsur: Our kind comes up before the police magistrate--and the highest we _ever_ get is the criminal court.
Liliom: Will it be the same in the next world?
Ficsur: Just the same.
Ficsur: We'll come up before a police magistrate, same as we did in this world.
Liliom: A police magistrate?
Ficsur: Sure.
Ficsur: For the rich folks--the Heavenly Court.
Ficsur: For us poor people--only a police magistrate.
Ficsur: For the rich folks--fine music and angels.
Ficsur: For us----
Liliom: For us?
Ficsur: For us, my son, there's only justice.
Ficsur: In the next world there'll be lots of justice, yes, nothing but justice.
Ficsur: And where there's justice there must be police magistrates; and where there're police magistrates, people like us get---LILIOM [_Interrupting._] Good evening.
Ficsur: Excuse me, sir, can you tell me the time?
Ficsur: [_Lays his hand over his heart._] FICSUR What do you put your hand there for?
Liliom: My heart is jumping--under the knife.
Ficsur: Put it on the other side then.
Ficsur: [_Looks out at the sky._] It's time we started--we'll walk slow---LILIOM It's too early.
Ficsur: Come on.
Ficsur: [_As they are about to go, JULIE appears in the doorway at back, obstructing the way._] JULIE Where are you going with him?
Liliom: Where am I going with him?
Julie: Stay home.
Julie: Stay home.
Julie: It's going to rain soon, and you'll get wet.
Ficsur: It won't rain.
Julie: How do you know?
Ficsur: I always get notice in advance.
Julie: Stay home.
Julie: This evening the carpenter's coming.
Julie: I've asked him to give you work.
Liliom: I'm not a carpenter.
[_More and more anxious, though she tries to conceal it._]
Julie: Stay home.
Julie: Marie's coming with her intended to have their picture taken.
Julie: She wants to introduce us to her intended husband.
Liliom: I've seen enough intended husbands----
Julie: Stay home.
Julie: Marie's bringing some money, and I'll give it all to you.
[_Approaching the door._]
Liliom: I'm going--for a walk--with Ficsur.
Liliom: We'll be right back.
[_Forcing a smile to keep back her tears._]
Julie: If you stay home, I'll get you a glass of beer--or wine, if you prefer.
Ficsur: Coming or not?
Julie: I'm not angry with you any more for hitting me.
[_Gruffly, but his gruffness is simulated to hide the fact that he cannot bear the sight of her suffering._]
Liliom: Stand out of the way--or I'll---- [_He clenches his fist._] Let me out!
[_Trembling._]
Julie: What have you got under your coat?
[_Produces from his pocket a greasy pack of cards._]
Liliom: Cards.
[_Trembling, speaks very low._]
Julie: What's under your coat?
Liliom: Let me out!
[_Obstructing the way.
Julie: Speaks quickly, eagerly, in a last effort to detain him._] Marie's intended knows about a place for a married couple without children to be caretakers of a house on Arader Street.
Julie: Rent free, a kitchen of your own, and the privilege of keeping chickens---LILIOM Get out of the way!
[_JULIE stands aside.
LILIOM exits.
FICSUR follows him.
JULIE remains standing meditatively in the doorway.
MOTHER HOLLUNDER comes out of the kitchen._]
Julie: I can't find my kitchen knife anywhere.
Julie: Have you seen anything of it?
[_Horrified._]
Julie: No.
Julie: It was on the kitchen table just a few minutes ago.
Julie: No one was in there except Liliom.
Julie: He didn't take it.
Julie: MOTHER HOLLUNDER No one else was in there.
Julie: What would Liliom want with a kitchen knife?
Julie: He'd sell it and spend the money on drink.
Julie: It just so happens--see how unjust you are to him--it just so happens that I went through all of Liliom's pockets just now--I wanted to see if he had any money on him.
Julie: But he had nothing but a pack of cards.
Julie: MOTHER HOLLUNDER [_Returns to the kitchen, grumbling._] Cards in his pocket--cards!
Julie: The fine gentlemen have evidently gone off to their club to play a little game.
[_She exits.
Julie: After a pause MARIE, happy and beaming, appears in the doorway at back, and enters, followed by WOLF._] MARIE Here we are!
Julie: [_She takes WOLF by the hand and leads him, grinning shyly, to JULIE, who has turned at her call._] Hello!
Julie: Hello.
Marie: Well, we're here.
Julie: Yes.
[_Bows awkwardly and extends his hand._]
Wolf: My name is Wolf Beifeld.
Julie: My name is Julie Zeller.
[_They shake hands.
There is an embarrassed silence.
Julie: Then, to relieve the situation, WOLF takes JULIE'S hand again and shakes it vigorously._] MARIE Well--this is Wolf.
Wolf: Yes.
Julie: Yes.
Julie: [_Another awkward silence._] MARIE Where is Liliom?
Wolf: Yes, where is your husband?
Julie: He's out.
Marie: Where?
Julie: Just for a walk.
Marie: Is he?
Julie: Yes.
Wolf: Oh!
Wolf: [_Another silence._] MARIE Wolf's got a new place.
Wolf: After the first of the month he won't have to stand outside any more.
Wolf: He's going to work in a club after the first of the month.
[_Apologetically._]
Wolf: She don't know yet how to explain these things just right--hehehe---- Beginning the first I'm to be second steward at the Burger Club--a good job, if one conducts oneself properly.
Julie: Yes?
Wolf: The pay--is quite good--but the main thing is the tips.
Wolf: When they play cards there's always a bit for the steward.
Wolf: The tips, I may say, amount to twenty, even thirty kronen every night.

[_JULIE does not answer._] I say--has your husband been dead a long time?
A long time.
What did he die of?
[_JULIE is silent._] LOUISE No one knows.
He went to America to work and he died there--in the hospital.
Poor father, I never knew him.
He went to America?
Yes, before I was born.
To America?
Why do you ask so many questions?
Did you know him, perhaps?
[_Puts the plate down._]
Heaven knows!
I've known so many people.
Maybe I knew him, too.
Well, if you knew him, leave him and us in peace with your questions.
He went to America and died there.
That's all there is to tell.
All right.
All right.
Don't be angry with me.
I didn't mean any harm.
[_There is a pause._] LOUISE My father was a very handsome man.
Don't talk so much.
Did I say anything----?
Surely the little orphan can say that about her father.
My father could juggle so beautifully with three ivory balls that people used to advise him to go on the stage.
Who told you that?
Uncle Wolf.
Who is that?
Mr. Wolf Beifeld, who owns the Café Sorrento.
The one who used to be a porter?
[_Astonished._]
Do you know him, too?
It seems that you know all Budapest.
Wolf Beifeld is a long way from being all Budapest.
But I do know a lot of people.
Why shouldn't I know Wolf Beifeld?
He was a friend of my father.
He was not his friend.
No one was.
You speak of your husband so sternly.
What's that to you?
Doesn't it suit you?
I can speak of my husband any way I like.
It's nobody's business but mine.
Certainly, certainly--it's your own business.
[_Takes up his soup plate again.
All three eat._]
[_To JULIE._]
Perhaps he knew father, too.
Ask him, if you like.
[_Crosses to LILIOM.
He stands up._] Did you know my father?
[_LILIOM nods.
LOUISE addresses her mother._] Yes, he knew him.
[_Rises._]
You knew Andreas Zavocky?
Liliom?
Yes. LOUISE
Was he really a very handsome man?
I wouldn't exactly say handsome.
[_Confidently._]
But he was an awfully good man, wasn't he?
He wasn't so good, either.
As far as I know he was what they called a clown, a barker in a carousel.
[_Pleased._]
Did he tell funny jokes?
Lots of 'em.
And he sang funny songs, too.
In the carousel?
Yes--but he was something of a bully, too.
He'd fight anyone.
He even hit your dear little mother.
That's a lie.
It's true.
Aren't you ashamed to tell the child such awful things about her father?
Get out of here, you shameless liar.
Eats our soup and our bread and has the impudence to slander our dead!
I didn't mean--I----
What right have you to tell lies to the child?
Take that plate, Louise, and let him be on his way.
If he wasn't such a hungry-looking beggar, I'd put him out myself.
[_LOUISE takes the plate out of his hand._] LILIOM So he didn't hit you?
No, never.
He was always good to me.
[_Whispers._]
Did he tell funny stories, too?
Yes, and _such_ funny ones.
Don't speak to him any more.
In God's name, go.
In God's name.
[_JULIE resumes her seat at the table and eats._] LILIOM If you please, Miss--I have a pack of cards in my pocket.
And if you like, I'll show you some tricks that'll make you split your sides laughing.
[_LOUISE holds LILIOM'S plate in her left hand.
With her right she reaches out and holds the garden gate shut._] Let me in, just a little way, Miss, and I'll do the tricks for you.
Go, in God's name, and let us be.
Why are you making those ugly faces?
Don't chase me away, Miss; let me come in for just a minute--just for a minute--just long enough to let me show you something pretty, something wonderful.
[_Opens the gate._] Miss, I've something to give you.
[_Takes from his pocket a big red handkerchief in which is wrapped a glittering star from Heaven.
He looks furtively about him to make sure that the POLICE are not watching._] LOUISE What's that?
Pst!
A star! [_With a gesture he indicates that he has stolen it out of the sky._] JULIE [_Sternly._] Don't take anything from him.
He's probably stolen it somewhere.
[_To LILIOM._] In God's name, be off with you.
Yes, be off with you.
Be off. [_She slams the gate._]
Miss--please, Miss--I've got to do something good--or--do something good--a good deed---LOUISE [_Pointing with her right hand._] That's the way out.
Miss----
Get out!
Miss!
[_Looks up at her suddenly and slaps her extended hand, so that the slap resounds loudly._] LOUISE Mother!
[_Looks dazedly at LILIOM, who bows his head dismayed, forlorn.
JULIE rises and looks at LILIOM in astonishment.
There is a long pause._]
[_Comes over to them slowly._]
What's the matter here?
[_Bewildered, does not take her eyes off LILIOM._]
Mother--the man--he hit me--on the hand--hard--I heard the sound of it--but it didn't hurt--mother--it didn't hurt--it was like a caress--as if he had just touched my hand tenderly.
[_She hides behind JULIE.
LILIOM sulkily raises his head and looks at JULIE._]
[_Softly._]
Go, my child.
Go into the house.
Go. LOUISE [_Going._] But mother--I'm afraid--it sounded so loud---- [_Weepingly._] And it didn't hurt at all--just as if he'd--kissed my hand instead--mother!
[_She hides her face._] JULIE Go in, my child, go in.
[_LOUISE goes slowly into the house.
JULIE watches her until she has disappeared, then turns slowly to LILIOM._] JULIE You struck my child.
Yes--I struck her.
Is that what you came for, to strike my child?
No--I didn't come for that--but I did strike her--and now I'm going back.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, who are you?
[_Simply._]
A poor, tired beggar who came a long way and who was hungry.
And I took your soup and bread and I struck your child.
Are you angry with me?
[_Her hand on her heart; fearfully, wonderingly._]
Jesus protect me--I don't understand it--I'm not angry--not angry at all---- [_LILIOM goes to the doorway and leans against the doorpost, his back to the audience.
JULIE goes to the table and sits._]
Louise!
[_LOUISE comes out of the house._] Sit down, dear, we'll finish eating.
Has he gone?
Yes.
[_They are both seated at the table.
LOUISE, her head in her hands, is staring into space._] Why don't you eat, dear?
What has happened, mother?
Nothing, my child.
[_The HEAVENLY POLICEMEN appear outside.
LILIOM walks slowly off at left.
The FIRST POLICEMAN makes a deploring gesture.
Both shake their heads deploringly and follow LILIOM slowly off at left._] LOUISE Mother, dear, why won't you tell me?
What is there to tell you, child?
Nothing has happened.
We were peacefully eating, and a beggar came who talked of bygone days, and then I thought of your father.
My father?
Your father--Liliom.
[_There is a pause._] LOUISE Mother--tell me--has it ever happened to you--has anyone ever hit you--without hurting you in the least?
Yes, my child.
It has happened to me, too.
[_There is a pause._] LOUISE Is it possible for someone to hit you--hard like that--real loud and hard--and not hurt you at all?
It is possible, dear--that someone may beat you and beat you and beat you,--and not hurt you at all.---- [_There is a pause.
Nearby an organ-grinder has stopped.
The music of his organ begins._]
